Industrial Law - organizations - rules - amendment of rules - compliance with procedural requirements - court's jurisdiction where Industrial Registrar has not given a certificate - control of committees of organization by members. Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 ss. 132, 133, 133AA, 139 (4), 140, 141. Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations reg. 115 (1) Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 s.24. Conciliation and Arbitration - Registered organization - Performance and observance of rules - Amendment of rules - Validity of amendments - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 (Cth), s. 141. Conciliation and Arbitration - Registered organization - Rules - Jurisdiction of Federal Court in relation to rules not certified by Industrial Registrar - Whether rules as a whole failed to make provision required by Conciliation and Arbitration Act - Requirement that rules provide for control of committees by members - Referendum power - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 (Cth), s. 55 - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904-1978 (Cth), s. 140 (1), (2), (3) - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904-1979 (Cth), ss. 4 (4), (5), 132, 133, 133AA, 139 (4), 140 (1), (2), (5D), (5E), (5G), (6), (7) - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth), s. 21 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1913 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1928 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1956, reg. 115 (1). The appellants, who included the general secretary and assistant general secretary of a registered organization, by separate proceedings that were heard concurrently, sought the following orders under the Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 ("the Act"): (1) an order that r. 11 (g) of the rules of the organization contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act; (2) an order under s. 141 of the Act that the respondents, other than the organization, perform and observe the rules of the organization by treating as null and void certain resolution of federal council purporting to amend rr. 11 (g) and 16; (3) an order that rr. 11 (g) and 16 as amended by those resolutions contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act; (4) an order that the rules of the organization generally, or r. 13A which dealt with the power to hold a referendum of members in particular, contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act by failing to provide for the control of the committees of the union by the members thereof as is required by reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) of the Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1956. The terms of the Acts, regulations and rules appear from the judgment of Evatt and Northrop JJ. The trial judge found that part of r. 11 (g) in its unamended form contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act and under s. 140 (5D) adjourned the further hearing of that application. His Honour refused to make the other orders sought. On appeal. Held: (1) Per curiam - As to the first order sought it was appropriate to adjourn the proceeding in which that order was sought to give the organization an opportunity to alter r. 11 (g). The respondents did not dispute the trial judge's finding. (2) Per curiam - The second order sought would be refused because r. 39, providing for the amendment of rules, had been observed as: (a) Per Evatt and Northrop JJ. - The relevant alterations to the rules made by the federal council were within the scope of or were incidental to the proposed new rule as endorsed and circulated. Daly v. Gallagher, (1925) QSR 1 , referred to. (b) Per Keely J. - The federal council when acting under r. 39 was not limited to the precise terms of the proposal endorsed by the branch meeting provided that the wording of the new rule or alteration decided upon by the federal council may fairly be said to have been proposed by a branch meeting and been forwarded at the appropriate time to each branch. (3) The court could not grant the third order sought because - per curiam - (a) The jurisdiction of the court to make an order under s. 140 of the Act was limited to those rules which have satisfied the requirements of s. 139 (4) of the Act, and (b) the amended rr. 11 (g) and 16 had not done so. Observations by Evatt and Northrop JJ. that under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 the court may in exceptional circumstances and in appropriate proceedings make a declaration with respect to the alteration of a rule of an organization for which a certificate under s. 139 (4) of the Act has not been granted. McLeish v. Faure [1979] FCA 38 ; (1979), 40 FLR 462 , referred to. (4) As to the fourth order sought - (a) Per curiam - The word "control" in reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) is to be construed in the sense of meaning the fact of checking and directing action, a method or means of restraint and not in the sense of directly controlling or commanding. Mackenzie v. Administrative and Clerical Officers' Association, Commonwealth Public Service (1962), 5 FLR 342 , applied. (b) Per Evatt and Northrop JJ. Keely J. dissenting, the court should not grant the fourth order sought as: (i) The court had to determine whether the rules of the organization made the provisions required by reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) and it was necessary to consider the whole of the rules including the method of electing the committees, the term of office of the members of the committees and the powers of members in general meeting. The absence of a power in the rules to call for a referendum on the decisions of a committee was not conclusive. (ii) The word control in reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) had to be considered in the context of the provisions of the Act and regulations currently in force. (iii) The rules vested the supreme control of the organization in the members and contained a number of express provisions by which the required control was made effective. Per Keely J. - Regulation 115 (1) (d) required provision in the rules for control "by the members" not control by the rules in some general way or by the Act and regulations. Income Tax - Assessable income - Taxpayer severing its connection as member with company - Taxpayer receiving its share of available funds - Whether assessable as dividend - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 44 , 47 . The taxpayer received a sum as a member of a company limited by guarantee (Ogg Holdings Ltd). Part of the sum represented part of a gift made to Ogg Holdings by a Mr Ogg, then one of its shareholders. Mr Ogg was the father of Mrs Slater, whose family company the taxpayer was. Another part of the sum represented part of the capital profits made by Ogg Holdings on the sale of a shopping centre. The sum was paid to the taxpayer in consequence of its retirement from membership of Ogg Holdings. The Commissioner assessed the taxpayer on both the above parts of the sum received as dividends within s. 44(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 . The taxpayer unsuccessfully appealed to the Supreme Court of New South Wales. The taxpayer appealed. Held, (by majority, Lockhart and Fitzgerald JJ.), appeal allowed. The taxpayer had severed its connection with Ogg Holdings and what it received was its share of the available assets. This was capital in its hands, and not assessable as a dividend. Bankruptcy: deeds of arrangement - whether deeds comply with the provisions of Part X of the Act - distribution clause in each deed purported to require the trustee to intermingle funds which were required by the Act to be administered separately - whether the court should declare each deed to be void or whether it should declare provisions of each deed to be void - conduct of registered trustee examined - circumstances in which a registered trustee should not accept appointment as controlling trustee or as trustee of a deed. Bankruptcy Act 1966 (C'th): SS108 ; 190 ; 222 (1), (2), (3); 237(2) Bankruptcy Rules Rule 100, Form 43 Bankruptcy - Deeds of arrangement - Whether the deeds comply with Pt X of Act - Distribution clause required trustee to intermingle funds - The Act requires these funds to be administered separately - Whether each deed to be declared void or whether distribution clause to be severed. Bankruptcy - Registered trustee - Conduct examined - Conflict of interest - Circumstances barring a registered trustee from accepting appointment as controlling trustee or trustee of a deed - Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth), ss 108 , 109 , 222 (1), (2), (3), 237(2) - Bankruptcy Rules, r. 100. In 1977 a group of medical practitioners, including each of the twelve debtors named as respondent to these applications before the Federal Court of Australia, embarked upon the business venture of establishing a private hospital. When they ran into financial difficulties meetings of creditors were held. In the case of each debtor an almost identical deed of arrangement was agreed to and executed by each debtor on 25 May 1981. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxation applied in each case for the deed to be declared void and to be terminated. At the wish of all parties all the applications were heard together. The full facts of the case including the text of cl. 3 of the deed of arrangement in the judgment is set out. Held, that in each of these cases the deed of arrangement is declared void on the ground that it does not comply with the requirements of Pt X of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) (the Act). Nor does it comply substantially, within the meaning of that phrase in s. 222(3) of the Act, with those requirements because: (1) In order to comply with Pt X of the Act, a deed of arrangement of an individual debtor must require the trustee to hold his contributions upon trust for his creditors, to be distributed rateably among them. Attorney-General of Ontario v. Attorney-General for the Dominion of Canada (1894) AC 189 , referred to. (2) The resolution proposed and accepted by each meeting of creditors was fundamentally based on the creditors receiving the fruits of the distribution prescribed by cl. 3 and granting in return the right to the release and discharge provided by cl. 4. (3) To use the power of severance so as to strike out the substance of cl. 3 would be to produce in each case a fundamentally different deed from that for which the creditors voted. Duties of a registered trustee considered.

Bankruptcy - property recovered or preserved by means of an indemnity for costs of litigation given by creditors other than the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation - Whether the power of the Court under s.109(6) of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 to make an order with respect to the distribution of the proceeds of that property with a view to giving the indemnifying creditors an advantage over other creditors is subject to ss. 221P and 221YU of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 . Bankruptcy - Litigation of bankrupt continued by virtue of indemnity - Indemnity provided by certain creditors only - Litigation successful - Deputy Commissioner of Taxation not indemnifying creditor - Claim of Deputy Commissioner to priority - Whether discretion of court subject to statutory priority - Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth), s. 109 (1), (6) - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss. 221P, 221YU. The official receiver was trustee of the property of the bankrupt. Early in the course of the bankruptcy six creditors, not including the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation, provided the official receiver with indemnities in respect of the costs of certain litigation already commenced on behalf of the bankrupt prior to the bankruptcy, without which it would not have been possible to continue the litigation. Subsequently the action was settled and after the deduction of certain costs and expenses the sum of $1,732.80 remained available for distribution to creditors. By application dated 14th August, 1980, the official receiver sought directions and orders pursuant to s. 109 (6) of the Bankruptcy Act 1966 as to the manner of applying the proceeds recovered by means of the indemnity for costs. The Deputy Commissioner gave notice that he intended to oppose the making of the orders sought on the grounds that he had a statutory priority pursuant to s. 221P (2) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 which could not be displaced by order of the court. Further by application on 22nd October, 1980, the Deputy Commissioner sought orders in relation to the net proceeds resulting from the litigation; the official receiver gave notice of opposition to the orders sought by the Deputy Commissioner. Held, that the statutory priority granted to the Deputy Commissioner of Taxation pursuant to s. 109 (1) of the Bankruptcy Act applies only to the distribution of proceeds pursuant to that section. It does not affect any distribution made pursuant to an order of the court under s. 109 (6) of the Act. In the present circumstances, having regard to the facts of the case, it was appropriate to give the indemnifying creditors the advantage over other creditors of having the whole of the sum recovered by means of their indemnity distributed amongst them in proportion to the amounts of their respective debts. Orders accordingly.

Administrative Law - Judicial review - Decision made under an enactment - Validity of enactment under challenge in High Court in separate proceedings by third parties - Decision attacked on grounds that decision-maker failed to take into account possible invalidity of enactment - Decision also attacked on grounds that enactment invalid - Whether a decision "under an enactment" - Whether decision open to review - Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth), ss 3 (1), 5 (1). The Taxation (Unpaid Company Tax) Assessment Act 1982 (Cth) (TUCTA Act) incorporates, by reference, many of the provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth) (ITA Act). Relying on s. 264 of the ITA Act, as incorporated into the TUCTA Act, the Commissioner issued a notice to the applicants requesting information about the sale of certain shares and seeking production of certain documents. At the time, the constitutional validity of the TUCTA Act had been challenged in the High Court in separate proceedings by third parties. The High Court had reserved its decision. The applicants sought an extension of time to comply with the notice until such time as the High Court delivered its decision. The Commissioner refused. Proceedings were commenced by the applicant under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth) Judicial Review Act for review of the Commissioner's decision to refuse the extension. The applicant claimed, inter alia, that the Commissioner ought to have taken certain matters into account, all of which were based on the possibility of the High Court holding that the TUCTA Act was invalid. The applicant also sought to argue that the TUCTA Act was in fact invalid and that the Commissioner's decision to issue the notice was therefore invalid. The Commissioner claimed, inter alia, that the decisions sought to be reviewed were excluded by Sched. 1, par. (e) of the Judicial Review Act, that he had no power to extend the time in any event, and that the applicants could not assert the invalidity of an enactment as a ground for review of a decision purportedly made under it. Held: (1) The Commissioner has ample power and discretion under s. 8 of the ITA Act (which provides for the Commissioner to have the general administration of the Act) to extend the time previously fixed by him for compliance with a notice under s. 264. Both sections are incorporated, by reference, into the TUCTA Act. (2) The decisions to serve the notices and the decisions to refuse the applicant's request for an extension of time for compliance are not decisions making, or forming part of the process of making, or leading up to the making of assessments of tax. Therefore par. (e) of Sched. 1 to the Judicial Review Act does not exclude the decisions from review under that Act. Tooheys Ltd v. Minister for Business and Consumer Affairs [1982] FCA 128 ; (1982) 42 ALR 260 , referred to. (3) A decision made under what purports to have been an Act of the Commonwealth Parliament is a decision "under an enactment" for the purposes of the Judicial Review Act, and it is therefore open to review notwithstanding that the only attack upon the decision is an attack upon the validity of the legislation under which it was made. This follows from the wide construction that should be given to the intended operation of the Judicial Review Act. Collector of Customs (N.S.W.) v. Brian Lawlor Automotive Pty Ltd [1979] FCA 21 ; (1979) 41 FLR 338 , per Bowen C.J. at 341-344; Sean Investments Pty Ltd v. Mackellar [1981] FCA 191 ; (1981) 38 ALR 363 , per Deane J. at 370-371; and Lamb v. Moss [1983] FCA 254 ; (1983) 49 ALR 533 , referred to. (4) The matters (flowing from the possible invalidity of the TUCTA Act), claimed by the applicant to have been relevant considerations which, it was said, the Commissioner failed to take into account in refusing an extension are certainly matters which he could have taken into account if he had chosen to do so. However, it has not been shown that he was bound, in the circumstances, to take them into account. The Commissioner's discretions to issue a notice under s. 264 and to extend the time for compliance with it are completely unfettered and it is a matter for him how he exercises them. R. v. ABC; Ex parte 2HD Pty Ltd [1979] HCA 62 ; (1979) 144 CLR 45 at 49-50; and Sean Investments Pty Ltd v. Mackellar [1981] FCA 191 ; (1981) 38 ALR 363 , per Deane J. at 374-375, applied. Ahern v. Deputy Commissioner of Taxation [1983] FCA 279 ; (1983) 14 ATR 807 , distinguished. (5) Because a decision of the High Court, to be handed down in the near future, will resolve the question of the validity of the TUCTA Act, it would be futile for this Court to hear argument on that question directed to showing that the decision to issue the notice was invalid.

A bankruptcy notice was issued at the request of the respondent against the applicant on 13 August 1982 based on a judgment in favour of the the respondent in the sum of some $334,000. The applicant claimed that he was entitled to damages for defamation by the Commissioner of Taxation, in a speech made by him at a symposium on taxation reform and he applied for a declaration to the Federal Court of Australia that the applicant has a cross demand against the respondent equal or in excess of the judgment debt. Held, that the application should be dismissed because the Commissioner of Taxation is not a servant or agent of the Commonwealth of Australia such that it is liable for any damages his words might bring as a verdict, and any verdict against "The Federal Commissioner of Taxation" or Mr William O'Reilly would not be a cross demand; it is not a demand in the same right as the entity entitled to the judgment debt namely the Commonwealth of Australia. Attorney-General for New South Wales v. Perpetual Trustee Co. (Ltd) (1955) AC 457 ; Baume v. Commonwealth [1906] HCA 92 ; (1906) 4 CLR 97 ; Enever v. The King (1906) 3 CLR . 969, applied. Andrews v. Income Tax - Deductions - Past losses - Insolvent company - Scheme of arrangement - Acquisition of shares in taxpayer by another company after years of loss - Channelling of business to taxpayer - Continuity of beneficial ownership test - Statutory interpretation - Application of amending Act - Whether "person" includes "company" - Whether s. 80B(2) (repealed) applicable for purposes of s. 80DA(1)(d) during transitional year - Mischief rule - Purpose of acquisition of control - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), ss. 80, A, B, D, E, 106B (3) - Income Tax Assessment Act 1973 (Cth.), ss. 8, 9(b), 23(3), 24(4)(a) - Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth.), s. 22(a). The taxpayer claimed in the tax year ended 30th June, 1973, a deduction for past losses. The commissioner refused the deduction, and this refusal was upheld by Sheppard J. of the Supreme Court of New South Wales. The taxpayer had incurred substantial losses in the two years after its incorporation. Within those two years, all the shares in it were acquired by Network Finance Ltd. and then further shares were allotted to that company. This meant that, under the then provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act, the past losses would be deductible from profits because the then applicable continuity of beneficial ownership provisions were satisfied. Profitable business was channelled into the taxpayer by Finance, and the commissioner allowed the deduction of losses against the profits. The relevant provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act were subsequently amended, the amendments taking effect for the next year of income. In particular, a new section, 80DA, provided that if voting control had been acquired for the purpose, or for a purpose that included, taking advantage of the loss carry forward provisions, then that voting control would be disregarded for ascertaining whether the continuity of beneficial ownership provisions were satisfied. The commissioner then applied the new provision with respect to the first year of income after its enactment, and refused Network a deduction for its previous losses. Among other arguments advanced on the appeal, Network contended that it was not a "person" within the meaning of the relevant part of s. 80DA, because it was a company, and the new section therefore did not apply to it. Held, that Network was a "person" because in s. 80DA the term "person" included companies. On the facts, the shares in Network had been acquired for the purpose of obtaining the advantage of the loss carry forward provisions. Network was therefore not entitled to deduct the losses.

INCOME TAX - Assessable income - Assignment of portion of taxpayer's share in partnership to trustee of family trust - Whether the consequence of assignment was to vest in trust relevant share of partnership profits for the whole year - Whether Commissioner of Taxation can nominate when partnership accounts can be taken - Delivery of deed in escrow - Creation of trust - Commercial reality - Equity and good conscience. INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1936 ss,92, 102(1), 102B, 161, 168. Income Tax - Income derived by taxpayer - Alienation - Assignment by deed of share of partnership - Assignee trustee of family trust - Assignor possible beneficiary - Deed executed shortly before end of year of income - Effect of assignment on distribution of partnership profits for year of income - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 92 , 102 . Held (per curiam): (1) Where a partnership agreement provided for the taking of accounts and the division of profits in July each year in respect of the year ended on the immediately preceding 30 June, an assignment by a partner during the year of income of 49 per cent of his interest in the partnership to the trustee of his family trust had the consequence that the assignee derived 49 per cent of the taxpayer's share of partnership profits for the full year. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Everett [1978] FCA 39 ; (1978) 21 ALR 625 at 629 and 655; Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Happ (1952) 59 ALR 382 at 386, referred to with approval. Rowe v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation (1982) 82 ATC 4243; Commissioner of Taxation v. Melrose (1923) 26 WALR 22 , distinguished. (2) Putting aside s 260 which was not argued in this case, the efficacy of the assignment for tax purposes was not affected by the fact that the taxpayer could, through the exercise of certain powers vested in him under the deed establishing the family trust, become a beneficiary of the trust. Arcus v. Inland Revenue Commissioner (NZ) (1962) 13 ATD 101 , distinguished. Corliss v. Bowers [1930] USSC 82 ; 281 US 376 (1930), not followed. (3) There is no principle that statutes imposing taxation should be construed in the light of commercial and economic "realities" rather than according to the "technicalities" of the law of real or personal property. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Everett [1980] HCA 6 ; (1980) 143 CLR 440 at 455, per Murphy J, not followed. (4) Section 102(1) had no application because the trusts upon which it was contemplated the trustee/assignee would hold the assigned partnership interest were trusts created on the establishment of the family trust by a person other than the taxpayer. Truesdale v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1970] HCA 27 ; (1970) 120 CLR 353 , applied. (Per Bowen CJ and Fisher J). For partnership purposes the Commissioner has no right to attempt to crystallise the net income of a partnership at a time other than that provided for either in the partnership agreement or by law (that is dissolution, death or bankruptcy). (Per Beaumont J). The date at which the profits of a partnership business are to be taken to have accrued depends upon the date at which they were ascertained or declared, or ought according to the partnership agreement or course of business to have been ascertained.

Income Tax - Deductions - Past losses - Insolvent company - Scheme of arrangement - Acquisition of shares in taxpayer by another company after years of loss - Channelling of business to taxpayer - Continuity of beneficial ownership test - Statutory interpretation - Application of amending Act - Whether "person" includes "company" - Whether s. 80B(2) (repealed) applicable for purposes of s. 80DA(1)(d) during transitional year - Mischief rule - Purpose of acquisition of control - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), ss. 80, A, B, D, E, 106B (3) - Income Tax Assessment Act 1973 (Cth.), ss. 8, 9(b), 23(3), 24(4)(a) - Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth.), s. 22(a). The taxpayer claimed in the tax year ended 30th June, 1973, a deduction for past losses. The commissioner refused the deduction, and this refusal was upheld by Sheppard J. of the Supreme Court of New South Wales. The taxpayer had incurred substantial losses in the two years after its incorporation. Within those two years, all the shares in it were acquired by Network Finance Ltd. and then further shares were allotted to that company. This meant that, under the then provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act, the past losses would be deductible from profits because the then applicable continuity of beneficial ownership provisions were satisfied. Profitable business was channelled into the taxpayer by Finance, and the commissioner allowed the deduction of losses against the profits. The relevant provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act were subsequently amended, the amendments taking effect for the next year of income. In particular, a new section, 80DA, provided that if voting control had been acquired for the purpose, or for a purpose that included, taking advantage of the loss carry forward provisions, then that voting control would be disregarded for ascertaining whether the continuity of beneficial ownership provisions were satisfied. The commissioner then applied the new provision with respect to the first year of income after its enactment, and refused Network a deduction for its previous losses. Among other arguments advanced on the appeal, Network contended that it was not a "person" within the meaning of the relevant part of s. 80DA, because it was a company, and the new section therefore did not apply to it. Held, that Network was a "person" because in s. 80DA the term "person" included companies. On the facts, the shares in Network had been acquired for the purpose of obtaining the advantage of the loss carry forward provisions. Network was therefore not entitled to deduct the losses.

Held: (1) That a taxpayer, who entered into a long-term commercial venture involving the growing of pine trees with a view to the future sales of timber therefrom, was entitled to a deduction under s 51(1) for a lump sum "management fee" paid to the managers of the venture in return for recurring services to be rendered in connection with the venture for a period of twenty-one years. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1979] FCA 29 ; (1979) 37 FLR 310 referred to with approval. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Ilbery [1981] FCA 188 ; (1981) 58 FLR 191 ; Clowes v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1954] HCA 10 ; (1954) 91 CLR 209 ; Milne v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1976] HCA 2 ; (1976) 133 CLR 526 , distinguished. (2) That the taxpayer's claim for deductions under s 51(1) could not be denied on the basis that the lease of land, on which the venture was to be carried out, was said to have been granted in contravention of the subdivisional requirements of the local legislation. (3) That s 260 did not apply to defeat or reduce any deduction to which the taxpayer was otherwise entitled under s 51(1). Cecil Bros Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1964] HCA 82 ; (1964) 111 CLR 430 , applied. Per Beaumont J (Jenkinson J agreeing): (4) That a taxpayer who bound himself, by enforceable obligations, to pay management fees and other expenses "incurred" those outgoings within the meaning of s 51(1), and the fact that payment was later effected by a procedure involving an exchange of cheques was not to the point. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65 ; (1953) 88 CLR 492 ; Nilsen Development Laboratories Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1981] HCA 6 ; (1981) 144 CLR 616 ; Australian Guarantee Corporation Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1984] FCA 240 ; (1984) 15 ATR 982 , applied. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Steeves Agnew & Company (Victoria) Pty Ltd [1951] HCA 26 ; (1951) 82 CLR 408 , referred to with approval. (5) That where, as here, parties to a transaction are at arms length and it is concluded that the moneys were outlaid by the taxpayer for a real or genuine commercial purpose, any inquiry as to the manner in which those funds were subsequently applied by their recipients is immaterial for the purposes of s 51(1). Ure v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1981] FCA 9 ; (1981) 50 FLR 219 , distinguished. (6) That, for the purposes of s 82KL(1) , when assessing the amount or value of an "additional benefit" which depends on what will happen in the future, an estimate must be made of the chances that a particular thing will happen and these chances must be reflected in the amount determined to be appropriate. Chaplin v. Hicks (1911) 2 KB 786 ; Howe v. Teefy [1927] NSWStRp 41 ; (1927) 27 SR (NSW) 301 , applied. The two applicant companies were trustees of trusts. The Commissioner issued notices to them under s 264 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 to produce certain books and documents. The applicants applied under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 to review the decisions to issue the s 264 notices. For the applicants, it was argued, inter alia, that the decisions were made for an improper purpose. Held: (1) The decision to issue a s 264 notice was a decision under an enactment. (2) The decision was not one within par (e) of Sch 1 of the Act as a decision making or forming part of the process of making, or leading up to the making of, assessments or calculations of tax. Deputy Commission of Taxation v. Clarke and Kann [1984] FCA 94 ; (1984) 1 FCR 322 , followed. (3) The decisions to enquire into the income of the taxpayers and the decision to require production of the documents referred to in the s 264 notice were not, except to the extent to which they merged with the decision to issue the notice, decisions to which the Act applied. (4) The rules of natural justice do not apply to a decision of the Commissioner to issue a s 264 notice. Income Tax - Administrative law - appeal - review of decision of the Commissioner of Taxation - whether the duties specifically imposed on the Commissioner of Taxation by regulation 35 of the Income Tax Regulations are expanded by s. 25D of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 - whether the appellant is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of that expression in the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 . Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 : sub-s. 3(4), ss. 5 , 13 . Acts Interpretation Act 1901 : ss. 25D , 46 (a). Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 : ss. 185, 186, 187, 188, 189, 190. Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 : s. 28. Acts Interpretation Amendment Act 1984 Income Tax Regulations : reg. 35. Income Tax - Objections and Appeals - Reference to Board of Review - Commissioner's duty to supply reasons for disallowance of taxpayer's claim - Interval between disallowance of claim and requirement to supply reasons - Existence of general statutory obligation of disclosure on decision-makers - Whether Commissioner bound to disclose findings of fact and material upon which based - Whether taxpayer a "person aggrieved" by Commissioner's refusal to disclose - Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth), s 5 - Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth), s 25D - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), s 186 - Income Tax Regulations (Cth), reg 35. Administrative Law - Person "making a decision" - Decision-maker required to give reasons - Interval between decision and requirement to give reasons - Whether decision-maker still in process of "making a decision" when giving reasons - Whether nexus required between the two steps for operation of statutory requirement to disclose findings of fact and material upon which based - Nature of Nexus - Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth), s 25D. Held: Per Lockhart & Wilcox JJ. (Smithers J. dissenting): (1) When the Commissioner of Taxation, in compliance with reg 35 of the Income Tax Regulations , supplies a statement of his reasons for disallowing a taxpayer's claim, he is not obliged by s 25D of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 to set out his findings on material questions of fact or refer to material on which his findings were based. (2) Section 25D contemplates a nexus between the making of the decision and the giving of written reasons for it, in the sense that the two steps must be of the one function of the decision-making process where the giving of reasons must be essentially for the benefit of persons affected by the decision. Under reg 35(1), however, the Commissioner is not involved in the process of decision-making; he simply furnishes information about a past decision to a statutory tribunal, a copy of which he is required to furnish to the taxpayer. Sutton v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1959] HCA 3 ; (1959) 100 CLR 518 ; R. v. Cain; Ex parte Evatt [1975] HCA 57 ; (1975) 133 CLR 37 , referred to with approval. (3) Per Smithers & Wilcox JJ. (Lockhart J. not deciding): The taxpayer was a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of s 5 of the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 , by the Commissioner's refusal to disclose his findings of fact and the material on which they were based, and therefore the taxpayer had standing to bring these proceedings. Tooheys Ltd v. Minister for Business and Consumer Affairs [1981] FCA 121 ; (1981) 36 ALR 64 , applied. Attorney-General of Gambia v. N'Jie (1961) AC 617 , considered.

In an appeal against a decision of McGregor J who upon review under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 set aside a decision of the appellant (the Minister) not to issue a final certificate under s 124ZAC(3) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 in respect of a film The Return of Captain Invincible and to revoke a provisional certificate issued under s 124ZAB(3) of the Act on the ground that the film was not a qualifying Australian film within Div 10BA of the Act. Held: (1) Under s 124ZAD, even though the Minister finds in a film under consideration significant non-Australian elements, it is still possible for the film to have a significant Australian content. "Significant" means "important", "notable", "of consequence" and the task of the Minister is to examine the Australian elements with a view to determining whether in the light of those elements, the film does have significant Australian content. It is not a question of weighing up the Australian elements against the non-Australian elements, and reaching a decision according to the side on which the scales come down. Although the Minister is entitled to say whether he regards one of the matters specified in s 124ZAD as more or less important than another matter specified therein, he must not place undue emphasis on non-Australian elements, as he did here. (2) It is a consequence of s 124ZAD(c)(i) of the Income Tax Assessment Act that the authors, composers, actors, scripwriters, editors, producers, directors and technicians identified therein must also be persons who took part in the making of the film, which involves some active participation contemporaneous with the making of the film. If a scriptwriter who is truly the scriptwriter of a film derives his idea for the script from some written work, but no more, the author of that written work will not have taken part in the making of the film, and, accordingly, the Minister should have regard (under s 124ZAD(c)(i)) only to the nationality and place of residence of the scriptwriter and not of the author, although he would be entitled to have regard to the nationality of an author who did not participate in the making of the film under s 124ZAD(f). (3) Where the Minister has issued a provisional certificate under s 124ZAB(3) of the Act but intends not to issue a final certificate and particularly where expenditure has been incurred in reliance on that provisional certificate, the Minister, upon conveying that intention by letter to the appropriate person, is bound by the rules of natural justice to make clear with some precision the nature and contents of any material which disposed him to refuse to grant the final certificate. On this basis, submissions in a departmental minute and by the Australian Feature Films Directors' Association Ltd should have been put to the respondents. R v. Gaming Board for Great Britain; Ex parte Bendim and Khaida [1970] EWCA Civ 7 ; (1970) 2 QB 417 ; In re Pergamon Press Ltd (1971) Ch 388 ; Herring v. Templeman (1973) 3 All ER 569 ; R v. Secretary of State for the Home Department; Ex parte Mughal (1974) 1 QB 313 ; Wiseman v. Borneman (1971) AC 297 ; Sean Investments Pty Ltd v. MacKellar [1981] FCA 191 ; (1981) 38 ALR 363 , referred to.

Bankruptcy Notice - Application for declaration that judgment debtor has set off, cross demand or counter claim equal to or in excess of the judgment on which Bankruptcy Notice based - that cross demand etc. could not have been set-up in the action in which judgment obtained - alleged defamation by the Commissioner of Taxation - whether Commissioner of Taxation servant or agent of the Commonwealth of Australia - Commissioner of Taxation a public officer holding an independent public office - claims not in the same right - amount of any verdict in action for defamation. Bankruptcy Act 1966 s.40(1)(g) Taxation Administration Act 1953 s.4 s. 8 Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 s.166 Bankruptcy - Bankruptcy notice - Notice based on judgment debt in favour of Deputy Commissioner of Taxation - Application for declaration that judgment debtor has cross demand - Alleged defamation of debtor by Commissioner of Taxation - Whether Commissioner servant or agent of Commonwealth - Whether Commissioner independent public officer - Whether Commissioner was acting in course of employment - Whether cross demand in the same right - Whether cross demand would equal or exceed judgment debt - Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth), s. 40(1)(g) - Taxation Administration Act 1953 (Cth), ss 4 , 6 , 8 - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), ss 8 , 13, 166 , 208, 209. A bankruptcy notice was issued at the request of the respondent against the applicant on 13 August 1982 based on a judgment in favour of the the respondent in the sum of some $334,000. The applicant claimed that he was entitled to damages for defamation by the Commissioner of Taxation, in a speech made by him at a symposium on taxation reform and he applied for a declaration to the Federal Court of Australia that the applicant has a cross demand against the respondent equal or in excess of the judgment debt. Held, that the application should be dismissed because the Commissioner of Taxation is not a servant or agent of the Commonwealth of Australia such that it is liable for any damages his words might bring as a verdict, and any verdict against "The Federal Commissioner of Taxation" or Mr William O'Reilly would not be a cross demand; it is not a demand in the same right as the entity entitled to the judgment debt namely the Commonwealth of Australia. Attorney-General for New South Wales v. Perpetual Trustee Co. (Ltd) (1955) AC 457 ; Baume v. Commonwealth [1906] HCA 92 ; (1906) 4 CLR 97 ; Enever v. The King (1906) 3 CLR . 969, applied. Andrews v. John Fairfax & Sons Ltd (1980) 2 NSWLR 225 ; Field v. Nott [1939] HCA 41 ; (1936) 62 CLR 660 , referred to

Income Tax - Assessable income - Payments pursuant to Motor Accidents Act 1973 (Vic.), s. 25 (1) - Compensation for "loss of income in capacity of employee" - Whether income or capital - Comparison with common law damages - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth.), s. 25 - Motor Accidents Act 1973 (Vic.), ss. 13, 20, 21, 25, 32, 79. The taxpayer received payments under the Motor Accidents Act 1973 (Vic.). She had been injured in a motor car accident and had "suffered a loss of income in the capacity of employee by reason of the injury" (s.25 (1) of the Motor Accidents Act ). She received $2,371.20 in twenty-two payments over about nine months. The Commissioner assessed her on the payments as income. For the taxpayer, it was argued that the payments were of a capital nature because they were compensation for a loss of earning capacity. Jenkinson J. of the Supreme Court of Victoria held that the payments were assessable as income. The taxpayer appealed. Held, dismissing the appeal, that an analysis of the Motor Accident Act indicated that the payments were for the purpose of providing partial recoupment of lost income. Furthermore, from the taxpayer's point of view, the periodic receipt of the payments suggested that they were of an income nature.

itaa-1936:82KK.catchwords: Administrative Law - application for judicial review - Deputy Commissioner disallowed taxpayer's objection to assessment - application by taxpayer to Deputy Commissioner for particulars of his reasons for disallowance - Deputy Commissioner declined to provide information - whether that is a "decision" - whether Deputy Commissioner under any legal obligation, to provide particulars - general principles - application in the alternative for writ of mandamus. Income Tax Assessment Act, sub-ss. 82KK(4), 92KL(2), 177F(1), s. 186 Income Tax Regulations , reg. 35 Income Tax - Objections and appeals - Taxpayer's objection to And: DEPUTY COMMISSIONER OF TAXATION [1984] FCA 103 ; (1984) 1 FCR 328 Review or court - Commissioner refusing taxpayer's request for Administrative Law - Income Tax Commissioner under a duty to provide particulars - Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), s. 186 - Income Tax Regulations , reg. 35 - Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth), s. 7. The taxpayer's objection to his income tax assessment was disallowed by the Lockhart J.(1) Commissioner's decision on the objection gave any reasons for the non-allowance of a claim for a deduction made in the taxpayer's return or for the disallowance of the objection. The taxpayer requested particulars of the reasons for the disallowance of the objection, including the basis on which the Commissioner made any determination or formed any opinion relevant to the determination of the objection. The taxpayer claimed to require particulars in order to decide whether to appeal to a Board of Review, which could exercise afresh all the Commissioner's discretions under the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (Cth), or to a court, whose function on appeal was much more limited. The Commissioner refused the taxpayer's request. Held: That the Commissioner is not under a legal obligation to provide particulars of the reasons for the disallowance of a taxpayer's objection. This is so even though fairness requires that he should provide, in appropriate cases, sufficient particulars to enable the taxpayer to make an informed election between a Supreme Court and the Board of Review if the taxpayer wished to appeal. Bailey v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1977] HCA 11 ; (1977) 136 C.L.R. 214 ; Kolotex Hosiery (Australia) Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1975] HCA 5 ; (1975) 132 C.L.R. 535 ; Spence v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1967] HCA 32 ; (1967) 121 C.L.R. 273 ; and Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. McClelland [1969] HCA 72 ; (1969) 118 C.L.R. 353 , explained and distinguished.

Held: (1) That a taxpayer, who entered into a long-term commercial venture involving the growing of pine trees with a view to the future sales of timber therefrom, was entitled to a deduction under s 51(1) for a lump sum "management fee" paid to the managers of the venture in return for recurring services to be rendered in connection with the venture for a period of twenty-one years. Magna Alloys & Research Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1980] FCA 150 ; (1980) 49 FLR 183 , applied. Ferguson v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1979] FCA 29 ; (1979) 37 FLR 310 referred to with approval. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Ilbery [1981] FCA 188 ; (1981) 58 FLR 191 ; Clowes v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1954] HCA 10 ; (1954) 91 CLR 209 ; Milne v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1976] HCA 2 ; (1976) 133 CLR 526 , distinguished. (2) That the taxpayer's claim for deductions under s 51(1) could not be denied on the basis that the lease of land, on which the venture was to be carried out, was said to have been granted in contravention of the subdivisional requirements of the local legislation. (3) That s 260 did not apply to defeat or reduce any deduction to which the taxpayer was otherwise entitled under s 51(1). Cecil Bros Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1964] HCA 82 ; (1964) 111 CLR 430 , applied. Per Beaumont J (Jenkinson J agreeing): (4) That a taxpayer who bound himself, by enforceable obligations, to pay management fees and other expenses "incurred" those outgoings within the meaning of s 51(1), and the fact that payment was later effected by a procedure involving an exchange of cheques was not to the point. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65 ; (1953) 88 CLR 492 ; Nilsen Development Laboratories Pty Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1981] HCA 6 ; (1981) 144 CLR 616 ; Australian Guarantee Corporation Ltd v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1984] FCA 240 ; (1984) 15 ATR 982 , applied. Federal Commissioner of Taxation v. Steeves Agnew & Company (Victoria) Pty Ltd [1951] HCA 26 ; (1951) 82 CLR 408 , referred to with approval. (5) That where, as here, parties to a transaction are at arms length and it is concluded that the moneys were outlaid by the taxpayer for a real or genuine commercial purpose, any inquiry as to the manner in which those funds were subsequently applied by their recipients is immaterial for the purposes of s 51(1). Ure v. Federal Commissioner of Taxation [1981] FCA 9 ; (1981) 50 FLR 219 , distinguished. (6) That, for the purposes of s 82KL(1) , when assessing the amount or value of an "additional benefit" which depends on what will happen in the future, an estimate must be made of the chances that a particular thing will happen and these chances must be reflected in the amount determined to be appropriate. Chaplin v. Hicks (1911) 2 KB 786 ; Howe v. Teefy [1927] NSWStRp 41 ; (1927) 27 SR (NSW) 301 , applied. (7) Onus of proof in establishment and quantification of "additional benefits" under s 82KL(1) , considered.

itaa-1936:133.catchwords: Industrial Law - organizations - rules - amendment of rules - compliance with procedural requirements - court's jurisdiction where Industrial Registrar has not given a certificate - control of committees of organization by members. Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 ss. 132, 133, 133AA, 139 (4), 140, 141. Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations reg. 115 (1) Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 s.24. Conciliation and Arbitration - Registered organization - Performance and observance of rules - Amendment of rules - Validity of amendments - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 (Cth), s. 141. Conciliation and Arbitration - Registered organization - Rules - Jurisdiction of Federal Court in relation to rules not certified by Industrial Registrar - Whether rules as a whole failed to make provision required by Conciliation and Arbitration Act - Requirement that rules provide for control of committees by members - Referendum power - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 (Cth), s. 55 - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904-1978 (Cth), s. 140 (1), (2), (3) - Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904-1979 (Cth), ss. 4 (4), (5), 132, 133, 133AA, 139 (4), 140 (1), (2), (5D), (5E), (5G), (6), (7) - Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth), s. 21 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1913 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1928 - Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1956, reg. 115 (1). The appellants, who included the general secretary and assistant general secretary of a registered organization, by separate proceedings that were heard concurrently, sought the following orders under the Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 ("the Act"): (1) an order that r. 11 (g) of the rules of the organization contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act; (2) an order under s. 141 of the Act that the respondents, other than the organization, perform and observe the rules of the organization by treating as null and void certain resolution of federal council purporting to amend rr. 11 (g) and 16; (3) an order that rr. 11 (g) and 16 as amended by those resolutions contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act; (4) an order that the rules of the organization generally, or r. 13A which dealt with the power to hold a referendum of members in particular, contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act by failing to provide for the control of the committees of the union by the members thereof as is required by reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) of the Conciliation and Arbitration Regulations 1956. The terms of the Acts, regulations and rules appear from the judgment of Evatt and Northrop JJ. The trial judge found that part of r. 11 (g) in its unamended form contravened s. 140 (1) of the Act and under s. 140 (5D) adjourned the further hearing of that application. His Honour refused to make the other orders sought. On appeal. Held: (1) Per curiam - As to the first order sought it was appropriate to adjourn the proceeding in which that order was sought to give the organization an opportunity to alter r. 11 (g). The respondents did not dispute the trial judge's finding. (2) Per curiam - The second order sought would be refused because r. 39, providing for the amendment of rules, had been observed as: (a) Per Evatt and Northrop JJ. - The relevant alterations to the rules made by the federal council were within the scope of or were incidental to the proposed new rule as endorsed and circulated. Daly v. Gallagher, (1925) QSR 1 , referred to. (b) Per Keely J. - The federal council when acting under r. 39 was not limited to the precise terms of the proposal endorsed by the branch meeting provided that the wording of the new rule or alteration decided upon by the federal council may fairly be said to have been proposed by a branch meeting and been forwarded at the appropriate time to each branch. (3) The court could not grant the third order sought because - per curiam - (a) The jurisdiction of the court to make an order under s. 140 of the Act was limited to those rules which have satisfied the requirements of s. 139 (4) of the Act, and (b) the amended rr. 11 (g) and 16 had not done so. Observations by Evatt and Northrop JJ. that under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 the court may in exceptional circumstances and in appropriate proceedings make a declaration with respect to the alteration of a rule of an organization for which a certificate under s. 139 (4) of the Act has not been granted. McLeish v. Faure [1979] FCA 38 ; (1979), 40 FLR 462 , referred to. (4) As to the fourth order sought - (a) Per curiam - The word "control" in reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) is to be construed in the sense of meaning the fact of checking and directing action, a method or means of restraint and not in the sense of directly controlling or commanding. Mackenzie v. Administrative and Clerical Officers' Association, Commonwealth Public Service (1962), 5 FLR 342 , applied. (b) Per Evatt and Northrop JJ. Keely J. dissenting, the court should not grant the fourth order sought as: (i) The court had to determine whether the rules of the organization made the provisions required by reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) and it was necessary to consider the whole of the rules including the method of electing the committees, the term of office of the members of the committees and the powers of members in general meeting. The absence of a power in the rules to call for a referendum on the decisions of a committee was not conclusive. (ii) The word control in reg. 115 (1) (d) (v) had to be considered in the context of the provisions of the Act and regulations currently in force. (iii) The rules vested the supreme control of the organization in the members and contained a number of express provisions by which the required control was made effective. Per Keely J. - Regulation 115 (1) (d) required provision in the rules for control "by the members" not control by the rules in some general way or by the Act and regulations. Rule 13A did not provide that control. (5) Appeal dismissed.

itaa-1997:83A-205.catchwords: Allders International Pty Ltd v Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps Commonwealth Constitution - Exclusive legislative power - With respect to a Commonwealth place - Characterisation of State law - Whether State stamp duty payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. Taxation - State stamp duty - Nature of stamp duty - Whether payable on a lease of part of a Commonwealth place. BRENNAN CJ. Tullamarine Airport was constructed on land acquired for the purpose by the Commonwealth of Australia. The Commonwealth remains registered as the proprietor of an estate in fee simple in that land. The Federal Airports Corporation Act 1986 (Cth) ("the FAC Act ") established the Federal Airports Corporation ("FAC") as a body corporate in which, pursuant to s 28(1) of that Act, Tullamarine Airport [1] was vested "without any conveyance, transfer or assignment". The FAC holds Tullamarine Airport "for and on behalf of the Commonwealth" [2] . It is a "place acquired by the Commonwealth" for a public purpose within the meaning of those words in s 52(i) of the Constitution . In exercise of its statutory powers [3] , the FAC granted a lease to the appellant ("Allders") of a shop at the Tullamarine Airport to conduct the business of a duty free and sales tax free concession. The instrument of lease demised the premises for a term certain expiring on 31 October 2000 [4] . The rent reserved was a fixed sum of $12 per annum (if demanded) plus a variable component calculated according to formulae the factors of which included the number of inbound and outbound international passengers and the average levels of their expenditure on goods to be sold by the lessee [5] . The instrument of lease was executed in New South Wales. Pursuant to s 32 of the Stamps Act 1958 (Vic) ("the Act"), Allders required the Commissioner of State Revenue in his capacity as Comptroller of Stamps of Victoria to express an opinion as to whether the instrument of lease was chargeable with duty and, if so, with what amount. In order to obtain that opinion, the solicitors for Allders lodged the executed lease with the Commissioner. The Commissioner expressed the opinion that the instrument of lease was dutiable and that duty should be assessed ad valorem on the rent calculated and paid in accordance with s 83A of the Act. Section 83A applies to a lease for a definite term of not less than 12 months where the rent cannot be ascertained at the time of execution of the lease. The calculation is based on an estimate and is re-calculated on annual re-estimates of the rent during the term of the lease. Stamp duty is chargeable on instruments pursuant to s 17(1) of the Act which reads as follows: " Subject to the exemptions contained in the Third Schedule and in any Acts for the time being in force, there shall be charged for the use of Her Majesty upon the several instruments specified in the said Schedule the several duties and additional duties therein specified." The Third Schedule provides,
